 ASK TBM Home › Business 101 22 minutes ago How Can Philippine SMEs Compete on Shopee and Lazada?
 By Rocky Teodoro Bookmark × Want to save this article? Bookmark feature is for subscribers only. Subscribe now to save your favorite articles. Subscribe now Already a subscriber? Login If you need assistance, please email [email protected] Shopee and Lazada's crowded marketplaces push Philippine SMEs into price competition. What determines profit are factors like brand differentiation and niche positioning.
 E-commerce in the Philippines is on the upswing, reaching $20 billion in 2026 and expected to maintain a double-digit growth rate in the succeeding years, according to the US International Trade Administration in June 30, 2026. Leading the pack among e-commerce platforms are Shopee and Lazada, with 91% and 88% usage, respectively, per a 2025 survey by HKDTC Research. 
 Many sellers, however, find that getting listed on these platforms is not the same as actually competing. The ease of entry for sellers on the platforms has resulted in crowded marketplaces where sellers compete intensely on price, reviews, visibility, and advertising. Marketplace take rates, or the fee a platform charges, are estimated at 3% to 12%, which can lower profit margins for small third-party sellers.
 Small sellers are drawn into reactive price competition, as the marketplaces reward low prices and promotional participation, while commissions, advertising, vouchers, shipping, and returns can consume much of the margin on low-ticket orders. 
 The Evolution of E-Commerce in the Philippines
 As defined by the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI), e-commerce is the sale or purchase of goods and services, conducted over computer-mediated networks. The goods and services are ordered over those networks, but the payment and delivery of the good or service may be conducted on or offline.
 E-commerce covers direct-to-consumer brand websites, marketplaces such as Lazada and Shopee, and social commerce, including TikTok Shop and live selling.
 In the local scene, e-commerce started out mainly in the business-to-consumer market, where the business managed the entire process from start to finish, including purchasing, website management, inventory and warehousing, fulfillment, payments, logistics, and customer service, according to former Zalora executive and Enstack CEO Macy Castillo in a June 4, 2017 news article.
 A major shift occurred with the introduction of Shopee, which provided a platform for smaller, more long-tail sellers to go online. These sellers could leverage Shopee’s third-party partners for payment and logistics while still having some control over their stocks and store management. Online selling became even more widely accepted during the pandemic, as entrepreneurs explored more direct sales channels to reach customers, moving e-commerce in the country forward.
 Prime Examples of E-Commerce Differentiation
 The marketplace model makes it easy for small sellers to get online, as the platforms handle many aspects of the process. A downside is that this also makes standing out difficult, as listings are almost identical to each other and price comparisons for similar products are easily done. Without differentiation, a product can become commoditized, driving prices down and reducing sellers’ pricing power. 
 Successful e-commerce sellers avoid competing merely on price and are able to differentiate on brand, content, and niche targeting.
 Homegrown beauty and cosmetics brand Colourette actively engages with its customers through the Colourette Club, which also serves as an avenue for product creation and innovation by listening to the users and in turning feedback into new products. 
 Fashion jewelry and accessory brand TALA by Kyla was able to turn an initial investment of P20,000 into a niche success by focusing on quality, innovation, and customization.
 Luxe Beauty and Wellness Group turned into a multimillion peso business through the use of influencers and social media for marketing.
 Operational Excellence Behind the Scenes 
 People may get into marketplace selling on the misconception that it is a low-effort, sideline activity that requires a small amount of involvement and time. The reality is that sellers need to focus on much more to compete in a crowded arena, including store management, fulfillment, content production, and customer service.
 Some sellers hire the services of e-commerce enablers because handling all of these aspects of online selling takes up a lot of time and effort. Great Deals Founder Steve Sy found huge success helping brands establish their market presence and grow their sales online, handling everything behind the scenes.

 How can Philippine SMEs compete on Shopee and Lazada despite high marketplace take rates?
 Philippine SMEs compete by differentiating on brand, content, and niche targeting rather than price, as Colourette and TALA by Kyla demonstrate.
 What is the BIR Registration Seal Badge requirement for online sellers in the Philippines?
 Under BIR Revenue Memorandum Circular No. 038-2026, taxpayers engaged in online selling must display a BIR Registration Seal Badge on their website, marketplace seller page, mobile app, or social-media business account to show proper tax registration.
 What government registrations does a Philippine online seller need before selling on Shopee or Lazada?
 Sellers must register the business name through the DTI’s Business Name Registration System, obtain a Tax Identification Number and register books with the BIR, secure a barangay clearance and mayor’s permit, plus sector-specific clearances where applicable.
 How did brands like Colourette and TALA by Kyla differentiate on crowded Philippine marketplaces?
 Colourette built the Colourette Club to turn customer feedback into product innovation, while TALA by Kyla grew a P20,000 investment through quality, customization, and niche jewelry positioning.
 Why do many small online sellers in the Philippines struggle to turn a profit on marketplace platforms?
 Marketplaces reward low prices and promotional participation , pulling small sellers into reactive price competition.
